title: The Silent Truth About Crossing a Black Hole
description: Contrary to popular myth, crossing the event horizon of a supermassive black hole produces no sudden forces or immediate destruction.

beats.text: You could fall into a giant black hole without noticing.
beats.visual: Illustration of an astronaut floating near a massive black hole event horizon

beats.text: Crossing its outer boundary brings no sudden jolts or crushing pressure.
beats.visual: Diagram of black hole gravitational light cone warping and event horizon

beats.text: That invisible edge is the event horizon, where gravity traps even light.
beats.visual: Event Horizon Telescope image of the supermassive black hole Messier 87, 2019

beats.text: Physicist Karl Schwarzschild first calculated this point of no return in 1916.
beats.visual: Portrait photograph of German physicist Karl Schwarzschild, 1916

beats.text: To a distant observer, your infalling body seems to freeze and fade.
beats.visual: Computer simulation of gravitational redshift near a black hole event horizon

beats.text: But space curvature around a supermassive black hole is remarkably gentle.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a supermassive black hole accretion disk and event horizon
queries: supermassive black hole accretion disk concept illustration
active galactic nucleus black hole jet illustration NASA

beats.text: Crushing tidal forces will not strike until you travel much deeper inside.
beats.visual: Diagram illustrating tidal forces and spaghettification near a singularity
queries: black hole tidal forces diagram illustration

beats.text: You would glide right past the boundary, completely unaware of your fate.
beats.visual: Chandra X-ray image of Sagittarius A* at the Milky Way center, 2019
queries: Sagittarius A* region Chandra X-ray image
